scenes.narration: Every time you open a website, your request crosses oceans and comes back in less than a second. How is that even possible?

visual.heading: How the Internet Actually Works
visual.subheading: From your click to the world, and back

scenes.narration: Over ninety five percent of data between continents doesn't fly through space. It travels through cables lying on the ocean floor.
When you type an address, four things happen. Your device asks DNS for the server's number. It opens a connection. It sends the request. And the server sends back the page.
Your data never travels as one big file. It is chopped into small packets. Each packet can take a different route. They are put back together at the other end.
Think of it like mailing a book one page at a time. Old phone networks reserved one line for the whole call. The internet shares every line between everyone.
Distance still matters. As a rough illustration, a server in your city might answer in ten milliseconds, one across the country in fifty, and one on another continent in about one hundred and fifty.
Along the way your packets meet routers that pick the next hop, switches that connect local devices, and data centres where websites actually live.
It started in nineteen sixty nine with ARPANET. In nineteen eighty three it switched to TCP IP. In nineteen ninety one the World Wide Web opened to the public.
At the twenty twelve London Olympics, the inventor of the web, Tim Berners-Lee, summed it up in four words.
So remember: addresses are looked up, data is split into packets, and cables under the sea carry it around the world. If this helped, subscribe for more.
